power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Calls for greater precision and mathematization in psychology are often motivated by the hope that they will help overcome the field's theoretical problems.
While mathematics undoubtedly contributes to scientific progress, this paper questions the idea that an increase in mathematization, in itself, constitutes progress.

First, it examines the tradeoffs of precision, arguing that making a theory more precise can change what is being studied, reduce its functionality, and sometimes lend an unwarranted authority to its claims.
It also considers examples of non-mathematical yet successful psychological approaches.
Second, the paper introduces the Mathematization Bind.
Under a realist standard, mathematical precision cannot, by itself, establish that a theory has moved closer to Reality, as the history of the luminiferous aether illustrates.
Under a pragmatic standard, the value of mathematics depends on what it enables us to accomplish, relative to the goals of inquiry.
Neither perspective justifies treating greater mathematization as scientific progress by default.
The paper also questions the tendency to regard an idealized image of physics as the model of scientific maturity.

It concludes that the appropriate role and degree of mathematization in psychology should be determined by what it actually contributes to 2 scientific inquiry, rather than by expectations about what a mature science ought to look like.
What I want to do is to change your attitude.
I want you to sense chaos where at first you noticed an orderly arrangement of well behaved things and processes.
-Paul Feyerabend (quoted in Hacking, 2000, p. 28) Psychology has no shortage of methodological reform movements.
text.formatted: -Paul Feyerabend (quoted in <ref type="bibr">Hacking, 2000, p. 28)</ref> Psychology has no shortage of methodological reform movements.

text.text: In the wake of the replication crisis, the field's attention has increasingly shifted beyond statistical practice to a deeper concern: perhaps psychology also has a theory problem (Eronen & Bringmann, 2021; Glo; ckner & Fiedler, 2025; McPhetres et al., 2021; Robinaugh et al., 2021), and many psychological theories are only weakly connected to the hypotheses used to test them (Fried, 2020; Oberauer & Lewandowsky, 2019; Scheel et al., 2021).
text.formatted: In the wake of the replication crisis, the field's attention has increasingly shifted beyond statistical practice to a deeper concern: perhaps psychology also has a theory problem <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Eronen & Bringmann, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Glo;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">ckner & Fiedler, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">McPhetres et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Robinaugh et al., 2021)</ref>, and many psychological theories are only weakly connected to the hypotheses used to test them <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Fried, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Oberauer & Lewandowsky, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Scheel et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: One proposed response to the theory crisis is to adopt a more structured methodology, often involving formal modeling to clarify and evaluate theoretical assumptions (Borsboom et al., 2021; Devezer et al., 2021; Robinaugh et al., 2021).
text.formatted: One proposed response to the theory crisis is to adopt a more structured methodology, often involving formal modeling to clarify and evaluate theoretical assumptions <ref type="bibr">(Borsboom et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Devezer et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Robinaugh et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: The reasoning behind such proposals is rather straightforward.
Ambiguities or inconsistencies in a theory are far less likely to be overlooked when it is expressed in an exact language than when it is left to the vagueness of verbal description.
Danielle Navarro's (2021) defense of mathematical psychology offers one of the clearest and most attractive versions of this position.
text.formatted: Danielle <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Navarro's (2021)</ref> defense of mathematical psychology offers one of the clearest and most attractive versions of this position.

text.text: Drawing on Shepard's law of generalization and its Bayesian descendants, Navarro argues that mathematical formalism can both clarify theoretical commitments and support generalization across contexts.

A mere verbal formulation of Shepard's law, which would state that the probability of generalizing a learned response from one stimulus to another decreases exponentially with their psychological distance, is not particularly useful in practice.
This essay accepts much of that argument.
The problem begins when a fruitful methodological consideration is inadvertently elevated into an ideal.
Greater precision can come to be treated as an improvement by default, with mathematical formulation representing its most developed form.
One need not explicitly claim that all sciences should eventually become physics, if they can.
It is enough to treat vagueness as something theories should continually overcome, or precision as something that should always be maximized.
The present argument challenges this expectation, rather than precision, formalization, or conceptual refinement themselves.
None of this disputes the need for better theory development and conceptual refinement, for instance along the lines discussed by Eronen and Bringmann (2021).
text.formatted: None of this disputes the need for better theory development and conceptual refinement, for instance along the lines discussed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Eronen and Bringmann (2021)</ref>.

text.text: Psychology should also make use of the full range of conceptual tools available, rather than relying on "statistical rituals" (Gigerenzer, 2018).
text.formatted: Psychology should also make use of the full range of conceptual tools available, rather than relying on "statistical rituals" <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Gigerenzer, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: If this is all that proponents of formalism and mathematical psychology are suggesting, then we are all in broad agreement.

This essay is particularly concerned with the possibility of a stronger but tacit claim: that mathematization is an essential part of any genuinely scientific practice and that a field should increasingly resemble physics as it develops.

This ideal may draw some of its appeal from a broader view that regards familiar psychological categories as obstacles to progress, and thus sees their replacement with more scientific concepts as a promising way forward (Churchland, 1981; Tu; mkaya, 2022).
text.formatted: This ideal may draw some of its appeal from a broader view that regards familiar psychological categories as obstacles to progress, and thus sees their replacement with more scientific concepts as a promising way forward <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Churchland, 1981;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Tu;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">mkaya, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: The concern here is less about whether such an outcome is possible and more about the "wouldn't it be nice if it were?"
part.
The essay takes issue with both this way of seeing science and the underlying desire for such an outcome among some academics in the first place.
This position, of course, is rarely stated in such blunt terms, and it would be unfair to attribute it wholesale to Navarro, Borsboom and colleagues, or many others mentioned in this essay.
Several of these authors explicitly recognize limits and trade-offs.

Nevertheless, the broader argument developed here considers how the admiration for mathematization is difficult to separate from a family of realist pictures of science in which progress consists, at least partly, in increasingly accurate representations of a mind-independent reality.
change what is being studied or come at the expense of functionality.
It also considers whether mathematization is necessary or sufficient for scientific success.
The argument proceeds from a broadly pragmatist perspective, although the purpose here is not to defend pragmatism against its philosophical alternatives.
It then examines the realist expectations underlying mathematization, using the history of the aether to question whether mathematical success necessarily brings us closer to reality.
Finally, it challenges the tendency to treat an idealized image of physics as the model of scientific success against which psychology should be judged.
Increasing precision often offers genuine advantages, but it can also come with tradeoffs.
or otherwise come at the expense of a theory's usefulness for the purposes at hand.
There are clear advantages to mathematical expression at least in cases such as Shepard's law.
In simple terms, Shepard's law describes how what we learn about one stimulus generalizes to other stimuli.
The more psychologically different two stimuli are, the less we tend to generalize from one to the other.
For example, if someone learns that one particular dog is dangerous, they may readily generalize that to a similar-looking dog, but not to a canary.

As Navarro (2021) discusses, it is the mathematical version, which specifies precisely how generalization declines with psychological distance, that allows for more exact predictions, among other advantages.

These advantages, however, come from specifying the phenomenon in a particular way, which in turn requires practical choices about what goes into the model. Guest and Martin (2021) argue that computational modeling forces researchers to examine and specify their intuitions, while also acknowledging that converting a verbal account into a model constrains the dimensions it can span.
text.formatted: These advantages, however, come from specifying the phenomenon in a particular way, which in turn requires practical choices about what goes into the model. <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Guest and Martin (2021)</ref> argue that computational modeling forces researchers to examine and specify their intuitions, while also acknowledging that converting a verbal account into a model constrains the dimensions it can span.

text.text: For present purposes, however, if the goal is to understand or explain a phenomenon, this can lead to a series of problems.
When there are discrepancies between an initial, often coarse-grained notion and a more fine-grained operational one, a decision eventually has to be made about which of the two should give way.
This becomes particularly important if the goal is to understand and explain a phenomenon assumed to exist in a mind-independent reality.

Researchers may continue with an operational definition because it works well with the available methods and theoretical framework, or they may continue trying to modify their models to better capture what the initial notion was meant to describe.
Sometimes the latter effort will succeed, and sometimes it will not.
The initial concept may itself turn out to have been misguided.

But the opposite error is also possible: researchers may struggle to capture a roughly correct initial concept within their mathematical framework and conclude that the concept itself is defective, rather than considering the limitations of their methods.
They may then abandon the original concept in favor of a narrower definition that is easier to accommodate within their existing framework.
Once this happens, making the resulting model more precise or more fruitful does not recover what was lost.
It may simply produce an increasingly successful account of the narrower phenomenon that the available framework made easier to study in the first place.

Unless realists are prepared to aggressively exclude from the list of real things anything that cannot be neatly captured in mathematical form, they must acknowledge the possibility that mathematization can lead researchers away from the very phenomenon they originally set out to understand.

On the other hand, if the case for mathematization is then limited to areas where doing so already works exceptionally well, then it becomes less of a general argument for mathematization and more of an obvious point: use math where math works.
A related problem is that translating an initial concept or theory into mathematical form can produce several different formulations, potentially leading researchers in different directions.

Van Rooij and Baggio (2020) for instance, despite strongly favoring formalization for making theories more precise, acknowledge that the same verbal theory can be formalized in different ways, potentially resulting in different theories and predictions.
This possibility is specially important here, although perhaps for reasons that go beyond their argument.
What follows from this depends partly on the researcher's end goal.

If the goal is to understand and explain, perhaps motivated by a realist account of scientific activity (i.e. something about science reflects a true structure in reality "out there"), then the question arises of which of these mathematical accounts, if any, should be taken as describing that reality, and why.
This is the classic problem of underdetermination (Stanford, 2023; Tulodziecki, 2017), which concerns not only existing alternatives but also possible ones that we have yet to encounter.
text.formatted: This is the classic problem of underdetermination <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Stanford, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Tulodziecki, 2017)</ref>, which concerns not only existing alternatives but also possible ones that we have yet to encounter.

text.text: Indeed, formal modeling alone cannot resolve the underdetermination that underlies the theory crisis (Oude Maatman, 2025).

It is worth noting that precision itself can refer to different things, such as numerical exactness, explicit theoretical commitments, finer descriptive resolution, and possibly other definitions that different philosophers find noteworthy (Koberinski, 2022; Strunz, 2012).
text.formatted: It is worth noting that precision itself can refer to different things, such as numerical exactness, explicit theoretical commitments, finer descriptive resolution, and possibly other definitions that different philosophers find noteworthy <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Koberinski, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Strunz, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: The notion of precision pursued in this essay mainly concerns concepts and constructs.
The realist picture considered here is one in which increasing precision is taken to help our concepts correspond more closely to something in an external, mindindependent world.
What that something amounts to can differ between different forms of realism.
For the scientific realist, this might concern objects, properties, and relations (Psillos, 1999).
text.formatted: For the scientific realist, this might concern objects, properties, and relations <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Psillos, 1999)</ref>.

text.text: For the structural realist, it would concern the structure and relations captured by our best theories, rather than necessarily the intrinsic nature of particular objects (Worrall, 1989).
text.formatted: For the structural realist, it would concern the structure and relations captured by our best theories, rather than necessarily the intrinsic nature of particular objects <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Worrall, 1989)</ref>.

text.text: For the entity realist, it would concern entities whose existence is supported by successful experimental intervention, without necessarily accepting the broader theories describing them (Hacking, 1983), and so on.
text.formatted: For the entity realist, it would concern entities whose existence is supported by successful experimental intervention, without necessarily accepting the broader theories describing them <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Hacking, 1983)</ref>, and so on.

text.text: Consider two reasons why a researcher might want to mathematize a psychological phenomenon or concept.
The first is pragmatic.
Mathematization might help us make better predictions, or accomplish something that was previously unfeasible.
The second is representational.

The researcher believes that there is something out there, with a stable structure that exists independently of our concepts and descriptions, and that increasingly precise mathematical specifications might progressively reveal that structure.

In this latter case, mathematization has an additional appeal: even when its practical benefits are unclear, refining a mathematical model may still seem worthwhile if it promises a better understanding of what the phenomenon really is.
This is not to say that a realist cannot accept that a concept becomes increasingly precise while still misrepresenting reality.

It is to point out that the additional value attributed to precision here may come from the expectation that we are also gaining knowledge about something in an external reality, or at least getting closer to doing so.
Without this expectation, precision loses some of its additional importance, with its value depending instead on the task at hand and other pragmatic considerations.
Ironically, a highly precise definition of precision would not change the argument made in this essay.

What matters here is the general intuition behind increasing conceptual precision: the more closely a concept can latch onto something stable in the world without catching other things along with it, the better it has supposedly become.
Think of a fishing hook with a specific bait, as opposed to a fishing net.
A perfect precision trap, drawing from the world exactly what is sought and nothing else.

Not only is there no reason to believe that such specificity is possible, even in principle, without presupposing a pre-figured world (Chang, 2022), but the relationship between precision and success can sometimes run in the opposite direction.
text.formatted: Not only is there no reason to believe that such specificity is possible, even in principle, without presupposing a pre-figured world <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Chang, 2022)</ref>, but the relationship between precision and success can sometimes run in the opposite direction.

text.text: Even for a realist, precision has to be precision about the right thing.
If making a concept more precise causes it to exclude relevant instances of the phenomenon under investigation, the resulting gain in specificity does not by itself amount to an improvement.
There are cases in which deliberately reducing precision leads to better outcomes.
A subway diagram, for instance, helps passengers navigate partly because it discards geographic detail.
Restoring centimeter-level spatial accuracy would make the diagram more precise while making it no more useful for navigation, and potentially less so.
In such cases, reasonable imprecision is part of what makes the activity possible in the first place.
Increasing precision can also, at some point, simply cease to tell us more about what we are trying to understand.
One can locate progressively smaller parts of a novel by identifying a chapter, page, sentence, and word.
Eventually, however, the relationship can break down.
A letter or particle of ink belongs to the physical text without containing any corresponding fraction of the story.
Of course, locating a smaller piece of text is not the same as making our understanding of the story more precise.
One might go further and argue that true precision was never about narrowing the target in the first place, but about capturing exactly what is sought, neither more nor less.
I shall return to this objection shortly.

For now, the point is that in practice this distinction can easily be lost when we begin with a broad, familiar concept as we often do and attempt to clarify it by breaking it down into more precisely specified components.
A label can be operationally precise yet conceptually empty or mainly irrelevant for practical purposes.
One problem is that mathematical presentation may make research appear stronger even when it adds nothing substantive to the argument (Eriksson, 2012).
text.formatted: One problem is that mathematical presentation may make research appear stronger even when it adds nothing substantive to the argument <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Eriksson, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: The critical positivity ratio provides a good example. Fredrickson and Losada (2005) proposed that human flourishing occurs above a specific ratio of positive to negative emotions.
text.formatted: The critical positivity ratio provides a good example. <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Fredrickson and Losada (2005)</ref> proposed that human flourishing occurs above a specific ratio of positive to negative emotions.

text.text: Using the Lorenz equations from fluid dynamics, they calculated a critical value of approximately 2.9, suggesting that people should experience roughly three positive emotions for every negative one in order to flourish. Brown et al. (2013), however, later showed that there was no adequate justification for applying these equations to positive and negative emotions, and that the mathematical derivation of the threshold of 2.9013 was fundamentally flawed.
text.formatted: Using the Lorenz equations from fluid dynamics, they calculated a critical value of approximately 2.9, suggesting that people should experience roughly three positive emotions for every negative one in order to flourish. <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Brown et al. (2013)</ref>, however, later showed that there was no adequate justification for applying these equations to positive and negative emotions, and that the mathematical derivation of the threshold of 2.9013 was fundamentally flawed.

text.text: What matters here is that the use of mathematics produced a high degree of precision through a fundamentally flawed mathematical procedure.
The added precision cannot be justified, for instance, by pointing out that 2.9013 made the claim easier to test or falsify.
The problem was not that the proposed threshold turned out to be inaccurate and that, thanks to the specific predictions it generated, we were able to find that out.
Rather, the mathematical procedure from which that precise value was derived was unwarranted in the first place.

I have no way of knowing whether Fredrickson and Losada's paper would still have been accepted without their attempt to apply Lorenz equations to a psychological concept and the "cool" impression the whole attempt might have made.

But contrary to Navarro's (2021) belief that psychological journals sometimes reject papers if they are overtly mathematical, I believe that the mere presence of status markers, including advanced mathematics or statistics, or even expensive, exclusive devices (e.g.
text.formatted: But contrary to <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Navarro's (2021)</ref> belief that psychological journals sometimes reject papers if they are overtly mathematical, I believe that the mere presence of status markers, including advanced mathematics or statistics, or even expensive, exclusive devices (e.g.

text.text: MEG as opposed to a humble scalp EEG), could increase the chances of an otherwise weak paper being accepted.
This remains an interesting open question that could be explored empirically.
Both possibilities can unfortunately coexist.
So far, I have argued that greater precision can sometimes change what a concept covers and lend authority to a model whose adequacy remains speculative at best.
However, excess precision can also lead to a loss of functionality.
Consider a clinical guideline stating that patients with condition X often report feeling unusually hot.
A patient might say "I feel hot", complain that the room is too warm, or repeatedly remove layers of clothing.
The patient could even make a joke about global warming.
A Martian practitioner following a strict lexical or behavioral rule would miss various instances of this symptom because it was looking for a very direct, precise report of "I feel hot".
Arguably, the ultra-precise version of the guideline would be easier to study systematically and quantitatively, since it would be almost fully independent of the clinician's interpretation.
That study could even use a great research design and sophisticated statistics and yet have little relevance to real life.
One might wonder whether the clinician could confirm the symptom, for the sake of precision, by asking, "So, you are feeling unusually hot?".
But this would merely move the problem one step back rather than solving it.
The practitioner must first recognize the original remark or behavior as grounds for clarification.
The demand for precision can therefore interfere with detecting the very instances that a coarser approach would have picked up better.
One might object that these examples mistake precision for narrowing a concept, or zooming in.
After all, wouldn't true precision describe exactly what is sought, and nothing else?
On this view, precision need not mean greater specificity.
The appropriate level of precision could itself be relatively coarse-grained.
For instance, if the task is to identify the sensation of feeling hot as a symptom of condition X, some flexibility and indeterminacy might be precisely what the task requires.
The problem, however, is that the appropriate degree of precision is now being determined by how well a definition serves its intended purpose.
A more specific definition that fails to serve its purpose is considered insufficiently precise, while a less specific one that works well can be called more precise.
But if this is what precision means, then saying that precision improves inquiry basically amounts to saying that something works well because it is specified in a way that makes it work well.
This move also makes the claim difficult to challenge with counterexamples.
Whenever greater exactness or specificity produces worse results, one can simply respond that this was not the right amount of precision.
Unless the appropriate level of precision can be identified independently of the outcome, precision provides little guidance about how an inquiry should proceed.
It becomes a retrospective label for whatever worked.
More importantly, this definition does not provide support for mathematization.
If precision means achieving whatever degree of specification best serves a particular purpose, nothing follows regarding the form that specification should take.
A verbal description or a mathematical model could each be more useful for one task and less useful for another.

Defining whichever one works as appropriately "precise" therefore cannot establish that mathematical form is generally preferable, much less that increasing mathematization constitutes scientific progress.
That would require a separate argument.
A related question is whether a framework can demonstrate its usefulness without having been formulated mathematically.
Dialectical behavior therapy (DBT) is a useful example of what a fairly non-mathematical framework can accomplish.

At its core, it combines two seemingly opposing ideas: helping patients change patterns of behavior that are making their lives worse, while also teaching them to accept experiences that cannot simply be changed.
In practice, this is organized around skills such as emotion regulation, distress tolerance, mindfulness, and managing interpersonal problems (Linehan & Wilks, 2015).
text.formatted: In practice, this is organized around skills such as emotion regulation, distress tolerance, mindfulness, and managing interpersonal problems <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Linehan & Wilks, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: The framework is deliberately flexible and principle-based rather than built around a highly structured protocol, allowing different components to be used or modified depending on the problem at hand.

Systematic reviews have found that DBT can produce meaningful clinical improvements in people with borderline personality disorder, which is notoriously hard to treat (Crotty et al., 2024; Hernandez-Bustamante et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Systematic reviews have found that DBT can produce meaningful clinical improvements in people with borderline personality disorder, which is notoriously hard to treat <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Crotty et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Hernandez-Bustamante et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: These achievements give the framework empirical and practical standing in its current form.

A clinician who has just successfully treated a case of borderline personality disorder may not be primarily concerned with the fact that DBT is not sufficiently mathematical, that some of its concepts may be imprecise and overlapping (e.g. fear of abandonment), or that they may be incompatible with concepts derived from the models of a mathematical psychologist working on emotions.
Moreover, it matters less whether DBT itself can one day become more mathematical and more precise in its terminology.
It already works fine.
Together, DBT and the positivity ratio illustrate that mathematization, at least in an extensive amount, is neither necessary nor sufficient for scientific success.
DBT illustrates the first half of this claim.
Despite being comparatively non-mathematical, its concepts have been developed into testable interventions with clinically important results.
Its scientific standing does not depend on first translating concepts such as distress tolerance or fear of abandonment into highly precise mathematical terms.
The positivity ratio illustrates the other half.
Here, mathematical form did produce precise and testable predictions, but the mathematical procedure responsible for that precision was itself unwarranted.
Taken together, the two cases give us little reason to treat mathematization as an achievement in and of itself.
Its value has to depend on what it actually contributes in the particular case.

Even if we set aside the preceding objections to precision, a further question still remains: why should becoming more mathematical count as a direction in which science, including the psychological sciences, ought to advance?
The Mathematization Bind (TMB) concerns two possible answers.
If progress means getting closer to a mind-independent reality, advocates of mathematization must justify why it should bring us closer to that reality rather than simply assume that it does.
If progress instead means improving what science enables us to predict or accomplish, then mathematization must be evaluated by its contribution to those outcomes.
Neither answer gives mathematization a privileged status in advance.
The dangers of pedestalizing mathematics go beyond overfitting or losing touch with reality in favor of "toy worlds", as elegantly acknowledged by Navarro (2021).
text.formatted: The dangers of pedestalizing mathematics go beyond overfitting or losing touch with reality in favor of "toy worlds", as elegantly acknowledged by <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Navarro (2021)</ref>.

text.text: Even in the positivity-ratio case, one could still point to errors in the mathematics and question whether plugging in Lorenz equations to calculate a threshold for human flourishing was warranted in the first place.
But what happens when the mathematics is sound, the theory makes a definite prediction, and an experiment supports it?
Can we then assume that the theory has correctly identified what exists, in part thanks to its mathematical form?
The history of the luminiferous aether gives us reason to doubt that.
The aether example is highly important because researchers without a background in the relevant fields are rarely taught about aether and, more importantly, what it shows about science.

The story is often framed as an illustration of Einstein's brilliance in introducing a paradigm shift in physics following the Michelson-Morley experiment, further demonstrating the triumph of science and suggesting that even when we (i.e. scientists) are wrong, further empirical testing and creativity will eventually point us in the right direction.
This essay does not share that optimism.
For nineteenth-century wave theorists, light required a medium in which to travel, just as other waves did, much as sound travels through air.
The aether was supposed to be that medium, extending through space and transparent matter.
Since aether was included in many scientists' lists of real things, physicists would naturally investigate its properties and its relation to ordinary bodies.
A moving body, for example, might carry the aether along with it or pass through it while leaving it at rest.
Disagreements about these possibilities could also be expressed mathematically and tested experimentally.
Even corpuscular theories of light were not incompatible with aether.
Newton, for example, suggested that light particles could create vibrations in a medium as they travelled through it.
These vibrations would then affect the particles' motion, making them more likely to pass through a surface or be reflected by it at regular intervals.
This offered a possible explanation for the repeating patterns of color seen in thin transparent films. (Newton, 1730).
text.formatted: This offered a possible explanation for the repeating patterns of color seen in thin transparent films. <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Newton, 1730)</ref>.

text.text: The existence of the aether was therefore a common starting point for otherwise competing theories (Swenson, 1972).
text.formatted: The existence of the aether was therefore a common starting point for otherwise competing theories <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Swenson, 1972)</ref>.

text.text: Consider light passing through flowing water.
If the water carried the aether along with it completely, then light traveling in the same direction should gain the full speed of the water, according to the ordinary rule for adding speeds.
If the aether remained entirely unaffected by the water's motion, light should gain no additional speed.
Fresnel proposed a third possibility in which transparent matter carried along only part of the aether.
His partial-drag hypothesis predicted how much the speed of light would change depending on the material's refractive index, a measure of how much light slows down in a given material.
The hypothesis thus provided a specific, testable prediction between the two extremes of complete dragging and no dragging (Cassini & Levinas, 2019; Stachel, 2005; Swenson, 1972).
text.formatted: The hypothesis thus provided a specific, testable prediction between the two extremes of complete dragging and no dragging <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Cassini & Levinas, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Stachel, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Swenson, 1972)</ref>.

text.text: In 1851, Fizeau tested this prediction by sending light through flowing water, comparing beams traveling with and against the flow.
When the beams were recombined, changes in their interference pattern revealed the difference in their travel times.
The effect agreed with Fresnel's formula rather than the prediction of complete dragging.

Although Fizeau himself remained cautious about accepting the proposed mechanism (Cassini & Levinas, 2019), the partial-drag account had now more going for it than a plausible explanation or equations.
text.formatted: Although Fizeau himself remained cautious about accepting the proposed mechanism <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Cassini & Levinas, 2019)</ref>, the partial-drag account had now more going for it than a plausible explanation or equations.

text.text: It had also survived an experimental test.
If the drag coefficient was taken to quantify a property of the aether with such mathematical precision, what did that precise quantification map onto?
Precisely nothing.

What followed was equally consequential for interpreting the role of mathematics when Lorentz later obtained the same coefficient within a theory in which the aether remained stationary (Cassini & Levinas, 2019).
text.formatted: What followed was equally consequential for interpreting the role of mathematics when Lorentz later obtained the same coefficient within a theory in which the aether remained stationary <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Cassini & Levinas, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: The question can be asked once more.

When highly intelligent academics disagreed about properties of the aether for decades, each presenting reasonable mathematical and empirical evidence in support of their view, what were they disagreeing about, from the perspective of understanding a mind-independent reality and its precise structure?
Precisely nothing.
A structural realist might respond that we should place our commitments in the mathematical relations that survive, rather than in things like the aether itself.
But how could researchers have known where to place those commitments before knowing the outcome?
Unless we have some independent way of making that distinction, this response risks becoming ad hoc (Vickers, 2017).
text.formatted: Unless we have some independent way of making that distinction, this response risks becoming ad hoc <ref type="bibr">(Vickers, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Whatever survives is treated in hindsight as what the theory was really getting right, while everything that was abandoned is retrospectively dismissed as unimportant.
The problem should be clearer now.
Physicists had precise mathematical predictions, explanations of how the aether supposedly worked, and experimental evidence supporting some of their theories.

Although some mathematical formulas survived into successor accounts (Cassini & Levinas, 2019), others did not, and even those that survived did not preserve the physical claims originally attached to them.
text.formatted: Although some mathematical formulas survived into successor accounts <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Cassini & Levinas, 2019)</ref>, others did not, and even those that survived did not preserve the physical claims originally attached to them.

text.text: Most importantly, the luminiferous aether was widely accepted as a real physical entity, yet this fundamental assumption about the world was later rejected as false.
Not approximately false or somewhat inaccurate, but completely false (Vickers, 2017).
text.formatted: Not approximately false or somewhat inaccurate, but completely false <ref type="bibr">(Vickers, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: According to our current accounts, there is no such thing as the luminiferous aether.
Mathematics certainly helped formulate the successor theories, but it was also an integral part of the theories they replaced.

The presence of mathematics alone could not tell researchers which account was supposedly closer to reality, nor could mathematical sophistication tell them in advance which parts of those theories would survive.
Suppose, now, that we judge a model by what it allows us to do, without worrying about whether it somehow corresponds to a deeper, underlying reality.
The case for mathematics then becomes dependent on the task at hand.
A mathematical model may be indispensable for one task and contribute very little to another.
What matters is how much mathematization helps us achieve our goals in each case.
The ability to express concepts and relations more precisely is not, by itself, a reason to prefer a mathematical approach.
Think of a simple analogy.
If all you care about is going from location A to location B, whether the vehicle is automatic or manual matters only insofar as it affects that goal, and no further.
You wanted to get to location B, and you got there.
This also changes how we evaluate the absence of a unified mathematical framework.
Several useful practices may address different parts of a problem (or a family of similar problems) without sharing a single set of concepts.
Their incompatibility does not cancel out what they each accomplish.
Unifying them might make them more useful, but it might also require giving up some of the features that made them useful in the first place.
Whether such unity is worth pursuing therefore depends on its costs and consequences for inquiry, an entirely pragmatic and empirical concern.
This is the bind.
Under a realist standard, mathematization cannot, by itself, establish that a theory has moved closer to reality.
Under a pragmatic standard, mathematics earns its value through what it allows us to accomplish, relative to the goal at hand.
In neither case does becoming more mathematical constitute scientific progress by default.
One might concede that mathematics guarantees nothing while still maintaining that it generally gives us better science.
The aether example shows that mathematical and empirical success can coexist with an entirely misguided account of what exists.
DBT and the positivity ratio show that the use of mathematics and fruitfulness can come apart in both directions.
To what extent mathematization improves psychological science therefore remains an empirical question.
Across which tasks, compared with which alternatives, and judged by which outcomes?
Indeed, if mathematical psychology did not exist, we might need to invent it (Navarro, 2021).
text.formatted: Indeed, if mathematical psychology did not exist, we might need to invent it <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Navarro, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: However, any stronger claim requires serious justification that goes beyond good examples from physics and mathematical psychology and also considers good examples of non-mathematical psychology and bad examples of mathematical psychology.
Trafimow and Fiedler (2026) discuss the familiar concept of "physics envy", examining features that might distinguish physics from psychology, including empirical laws, parsimony, and falsifiability.
Debates over these differences and psychology's supposed inferiority have persisted for decades (Howell et al., 2014; Meehl, 1967).
text.formatted: Debates over these differences and psychology's supposed inferiority have persisted for decades <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Howell et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Meehl, 1967)</ref>.

text.text: Much of this discussion asks whether psychology can ever become as successful as physics, or whether the nature of what psychology studies makes it unreasonable to expect comparable achievements.
When the debate is framed in these terms, physics is already granted the superior position, but perhaps for the wrong (or at least questionable) reasons.

Psychology's inferiority is, at best, tolerated and understood (for instance, due to the complexity of what it studies), in the hope that it might one day become more like physics: more unified, more mathematical, more objective.

This essay rejects that framing and questions why scientific success should be judged by mathematical form (or any other kind of form), or by resemblance to physics, rather than by the ability to solve concrete, well-defined problems.

Under a pragmatic account, any advantage physics has over psychology derives from its capacity to generate useful practices that serve our purposes, not from any privileged access to a perspective-independent reality or a God's-eye view.
The idea that science should aspire to reveal such a reality rests on a broadly realist conception of science.

As long as serious objections to that realist picture remain unresolved (Chang, 2022; Stanford, 2023; Vickers, 2017), this ideal cannot simply be taken for granted as the ultimate measure of scientific progress.
text.formatted: As long as serious objections to that realist picture remain unresolved <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Chang, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Stanford, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Vickers, 2017)</ref>, this ideal cannot simply be taken for granted as the ultimate measure of scientific progress.

text.text: Consequently, once theory evaluation is stripped of such assumptions, the treatment of mathematization in psychology follows suit: there can be a too little, a just enough, and a too much.
From a pragmatic perspective, the question of whether psychology needs more mathematics cannot be answered in the abstract.
It depends on what psychologists are trying to accomplish and what mathematics can contribute to those efforts.

Researchers should not have to justify the absence of mathematics in an otherwise successful approach, just as its introduction should not automatically count as progress merely because it makes a theory more precise or brings it closer in form to the theories of physics.
The same applies to precision, unification, and other characteristics commonly associated with scientific maturity.
Their value depends on what they enable us to accomplish, relative to the problems we are trying to address.
Those who instead favor a realist standard must explain why mathematical elegance should count as scientific progress beyond its practical contributions.
The history of science offers many examples of mathematically sophisticated theories built on entirely mistaken assumptions about reality.
What makes the present case different, and more importantly, how can we tell?
Simply assuming that the world has a discoverable mathematical structure, and that greater mathematization therefore brings us closer to it, does not answer this question.
The point is not to lower our expectations of science, including psychology, but to reconsider what those expectations should be in the first place.

Pragmatism offers a way of evaluating scientific progress without first (or ever) having to settle questions about whether our theories capture the true structure of reality, thereby avoiding endless theoretical battles that need not be settled for scientific inquiry to be fruitful.
If the goal is to make psychology a more successful science, mathematical form is neither an end in itself nor an ultimate measure of success.
It is one of the means available to us, which may prove indispensable in some cases, unnecessary in others, and even counterproductive in still other circumstances.
What matters is whether we are making progress toward solving the problems that led us to develop these theories and methods in the first place.
